papers.title: PVFormer: Proper Velocity Transformer for Stable and Scalable Hyperbolic Representation Learning
papers.label: arXiv:2611.30785v1

summary.one_liner: PVFormer is a Transformer that performs all three self-attention steps (transformation, similarity, aggregation) natively in the proper velocity model of hyperbolic space, aiming to keep the whole block intrinsic to that geometry and scalable to large graphs.
summary.plain: Many AI models store data as points in a curved space, which suits data with tree-like hierarchies, such as family trees or taxonomies. Building the standard Transformer (the attention-based architecture behind many language models) in this curved space has been awkward, so existing versions often rely on workarounds. This paper proposes PVFormer, which redesigns the Transformer's parts directly in a different coordinate system called proper velocity space, and reports that it works across graph, text, and vision tests.
summary.why: It addresses a real design gap: earlier hyperbolic Transformers used bounded coordinates or projection steps that can make them harder to keep stable and to scale. Whether this gives practical gains beyond the reported benchmarks is not something the summary text can establish.
summary.background:
- Hyperbolic space: a curved geometry in which tree-like data can be embedded with less distortion than in flat space.
- Transformer self-attention: a mechanism where each item compares itself with others (similarity) and then blends their information (aggregation), with a transformation step beforehand.
- Models of hyperbolic space: Poincaré and Lorentz models are common coordinate systems; the paper argues their constraints cause trouble.
- Proper velocity: an alternative, unconstrained coordinate system for the same hyperbolic geometry.
- Busemann score and midpoint: geometric analogues of a dot-product score and an average, adapted to curved space.
- Linear attention: a cheaper variant of attention whose cost grows more gently with data size, relevant for large graphs.

papers.abstract: Hyperbolic representations have shown remarkable success on hierarchical and tree-like data, and Transformers have become a central architecture for representation learning. However, a principled construction of hyperbolic Transformers remains challenging because the self-attention layer decomposes into three coupled primitives, transformation, similarity, and aggregation, that should all respect the underlying geometry. Existing hyperbolic Transformer designs are typically built in the Poincar\'e or Lorentz models, where bounded domains, time-like constraints, tangent-space detours, or projection steps make it difficult to keep the full block intrinsic and scalable. To address this gap, we propose PVFormer, to the best of our knowledge, the first Transformer architecture that operates natively in proper velocity (PV) space. The proper velocity model provides an unconstrained representation of hyperbolic geometry, and PVFormer exploits this structure to redesign the Transformer block in PV space. On the transformation side, we use PV homomorphism transformations to update query and value representations. On the similarity side, we generalize Euclidean inner-product attention with a PV Busemann score inspired by Busemann-based hyperbolic learning and a PV point-to-hyperplane key transformation. On the aggregation side, we replace Euclidean averaging with PV midpoint aggregation and further derive a scalable PV linear attention variant for large graphs. Extensive experiments support the effectiveness of PVFormer across graph, text, and vision benchmarks.

papers.title: Orthogonally Mixed Sign Coding with Progressive Residual Refinement for Transformer Weight Compression
papers.label: arXiv:2611.31089v1

summary.one_liner: A training-free, residual sign-based weight quantization method for Transformers that uses randomized orthogonal mixing to make residuals more Gaussian-like, evaluated on GPT-2 Large and Llama-3-8B.
summary.plain: Large language models store huge numbers of weights, and compressing them usually hurts how well they predict text. This paper proposes a way to compress a model's weights by repeatedly storing only the sign (positive or negative) of the leftover error, after first shuffling the weights with a randomizing rotation. On GPT-2 Large and Llama-3-8B, the authors report perplexity (a measure of how surprised the model is by text, where lower is better) of 32.16 and 12.73 after five stages, versus 29.89 and 11.07 for the uncompressed models.
summary.why: Compressing models without any retraining or calibration data would make them cheaper to store and run, which matters for deploying them on modest hardware. The text reports the accuracy gap at five stages and says ablations support the design choices, but it does not show how the storage savings compare in practice with established quantizers beyond a general claim of trade-offs.
summary.background:
- Quantization: storing model weights with fewer bits to save memory.
- Perplexity: a standard score for language models; lower means better prediction. Going from 29.89 to 32.16 is a measurable but modest loss.
- Residual coding: storing an approximation, then storing the leftover error, and repeating to refine it.
- Sign coding: keeping only whether a value is positive or negative, which costs about one bit per value.
- Orthogonal mixing: a reversible rotation of values that spreads information out so they look more like a bell-curve (Gaussian) distribution.
- Training-free: the method needs no gradient-based retraining of the model.

papers.abstract: LLM quantization reduces storage but often degrades predictive fidelity at low bit rates. We propose a training-free, CDF-free, Gaussian-CLT-motivated progressive residual-sign quantization framework that uses randomized orthogonal mixing to promote Gaussian-like residual distributions and improve sign based reconstruction of Transformer weights. Each stage independently normalizes residuals and analytically calibrates reconstruction, progressively recovering quantization errors. The framework enables flexible storage-fidelity trade-offs without learned codebooks, empirical CDFs, or trellis optimization. We evaluate GPT-2 Large and Llama-3-8B across attention and MLP projections. At five residual stages, joint quantization preserves near-baseline predictive fidelity, achieving perplexities of 32.16 and 12.73, compared with full-precision values of 29.89 and 11.07, respectively. Ablations further demonstrate that orthogonal mixing substantially improves reconstruction over identity-based sign coding, while activation-aware scaling improves output fidelity and reduced-precision statistics lower storage overhead with negligible perplexity degradation. Comparisons with conventional quantizers establish the method's progressive fidelity recovery and characterize its storage-quality and runtime trade-offs. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of orthogonally mixed residual-sign coding for flexible, training-free Transformer weight compression.

papers.title: Turnout: Adaptive Attention Switching for Efficient Reasoning
papers.label: arXiv:2611.27500v1

summary.background:
- Transformer: the neural network architecture behind most modern language models.
- Attention: the mechanism that lets the model look back at earlier tokens when producing the next one.
- Key-value (KV) cache: stored memory of past tokens that grows as the output gets longer; it is the main memory cost during generation.
- Linear attention: an approximation with a fixed-size memory that does not grow with length, but is typically less accurate.
- Linearization / distillation: converting a trained model to use the cheaper mechanism by training the new path to mimic the original.
- Hybrid model: a model that uses both full and linear attention in different layers.
- Reinforcement learning: training a policy by rewarding good outcomes; here the reward combines correctness and memory use.
- Pareto frontier: the set of trade-offs where you cannot improve accuracy without spending more memory, or vice versa.
summary.one_liner: Turnout converts a pretrained full-attention transformer into a hybrid that can switch each layer between full and linear attention at generation time, with the switching policy learned by reinforcement learning under a reward that trades off answer correctness against memory use.
summary.plain: Large language models remember what they have already written using a growing memory store, which gets expensive when they produce long chains of reasoning. This paper takes an existing model and swaps part of that memory for a fixed-size one, which saves memory but usually makes answers less accurate. The authors add a learned controller that decides, layer by layer and during writing, when to use the full memory and when to use the cheaper one, and report that this gives a better balance of accuracy and efficiency than fixed rules on reasoning tasks.
summary.why: Memory cost of long reasoning outputs is a practical limit on how these models are deployed, so a method that keeps accuracy while cutting memory could matter. The text reports only that the learned policy beats fixed-switching and static hybrid baselines on a Pareto frontier; it gives no specific numbers here, so the size of the gain is unclear from this summary alone.

papers.abstract: Post-hoc transformer linearization replaces the key-value cache of full attention, which grows linearly with generation length, with a fixed size state. This change reduces memory consumption but often hurts accuracy. In reasoning tasks, which require long generations, this effect is especially pronounced. In this work we introduce Turnout, a method that mitigates accuracy loss as a result of linearization, while maintaining its memory-reduction benefits. We apply post-hoc linearization to a pretrained full-attention model, training a linear path through distillation while leaving the original full-attention path unchanged. During response generation, the resulting hybrid model retains both paths and uses a learned policy to control when each layer switches from full to linear attention. We train the policy with reinforcement learning using a reward that balances answer correctness and memory use. Empirical evaluation of our method shows that the learned adaptive policy achieves a better accuracy-efficiency Pareto frontier on reasoning tasks compared to fixed switching and static hybrid baselines.

papers.title: MemOnce: A Scalable Memory Architecture for Large Language Models
papers.label: arXiv:2611.27973v1

summary.background:
- Transformer language models store a "KV cache": per-token internal values reused for attention, which grows with context length.
- Attention cost grows quadratically with context length in standard Transformers; linear-time models compress history into a fixed-size state instead.
- Hidden states are the internal numerical representations a network produces at each layer.
- Sparse attention means attending to only a selected subset of past items rather than all of them.
- Pretraining trains a model from scratch on broad data; post-training adaptation tunes an existing model further.
- Zero-shot generalization means applying a trained model to new tasks without task-specific training.
summary.one_liner: MemOnce proposes a language model memory architecture that caches a small set of final-layer hidden states, decodes them into attention KV caches on demand, and uses sparse retrieval whose indices are computed once and shared across layers, with reported gains in memory footprint, latency, and throughput at 1M-token contexts.
summary.plain: Chatbots and other language models normally keep a growing scratchpad of everything they have read, and this scratchpad takes up more and more computer memory as conversations get longer. This paper proposes a different way to store that history: it keeps only a compact summary of each part and rebuilds the detailed working memory from those summaries when needed. The authors report that, when they adapt a 4-billion-parameter Qwen3.5 model with this method, the stored memory shrinks about 1,313 times and the time to process a 1-million-token input drops about 6.9 times, though these results come from the authors' own experiments.
summary.why: Memory cost is a practical limit on running language models over long, continuing interactions, so a method that keeps detail while cutting storage could matter for that use. The text does not show how the approach compares under independent testing, so its significance is still open.

papers.abstract: Deploying large language models (LLMs) in long-horizon and continual interactions requires maintaining reusable memory states for future inference, posing challenges for existing architectures. Standard Transformers accumulate layer-wise, token-level KV caches, incurring linear GPU memory growth and quadratic computational complexity as the context expands. In contrast, linear-time architectures compress history into fixed-size states, but struggle to retain fine-grained details. We introduce MemOnce, a foundation architecture that learns scalable memory states for language models. MemOnce is based on two core designs: (a) Memory encoder-decoder: it caches only a small subset of final-layer hidden states as compact memory representations and dynamically decodes them back into KV caches for attention layers; (b) Memory sparse attention: for each continual input, MemOnce adaptively retrieves relevant memory representations, with the sparse indices computed only once across layers. Coupling these two designs enables efficient on-the-fly memory loading and KV cache decoding, drastically reducing the GPU memory footprint and achieving linear-time complexity. We conduct extensive experiments to show that MemOnce outperforms Transformers and other architectures across varying model sizes, context lengths, and training paradigms (pretraining and post-training adaptation). In particular, adapting Qwen3.5-4B with MemOnce reduces memory state cache by 1313$\times$ and prefill latency by 6.9$\times$ at 1M context, and improves throughput by 3.5$\times$ and overall memory performance by +5.77%. Finally, MemOnce generalizes zero-shot to downstream representation tasks, achieving competitive results against specialized models.
